title: High-field Josephson effect enabled by a moiré Hofstadter spectrum
authors: A. Díez-Carlón, M. Cárdenes Wuttig, N. Wei, D. Ivanov, P. Altpeter, P. Hakonen, K. Watanabe, T. Taniguchi, L. I. Glazman, D. K. Efetov
abstract: Magnetic fields generally suppress phase-coherent Josephson transport, limiting superconducting interferometry to relatively low fields. Here we show that moiré-engineered graphene Josephson junctions can overcome this constraint. Using ballistic graphene/hBN junctions, we establish phase-coherent Andreev transport through Fabry-Pérot oscillations and Fraunhofer interference that persist across both the primary Dirac cone and reconstructed moiré minibands. We then demonstrate phase-coherent Josephson interference up to 6 T in the fractal Hofstadter-butterfly regime, well beyond the range expected for conventional ballistic graphene junctions. Comparison with Hofstadter-spectrum calculations reveals that superconductivity survives where the moiré potential transforms Landau levels with quenched group velocity into dispersive magnetic Bloch bands with finite quasiparticle group velocity, enabling extended electron-hole Andreev trajectories across the junction. Our results show that Hofstadter minibands can stabilize phase-coherent superconductivity deep into the parameter domain conventionally associated with the quantum Hall regime, establishing a new platform for high-field superconducting interferometry.
summary: This work demonstrates that moiré engineering in graphene Josephson junctions enables phase-coherent superconducting transport far beyond the limits imposed by conventional magnetic field suppression. By utilizing the complex Hofstadter spectrum arising from the moiré potential, the system maintains finite quasiparticle group velocities even deep into the quantum Hall regime. This establishes a novel platform for high-field superconducting interferometry.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the magnetic field suppression of phase-coherent Josephson transport, which typically limits superconducting interferometry to low fields.
main_result: Moiré engineering in graphene allows for stable, high-field (up to 6 T) phase-coherent superconductivity by transforming Landau levels into dispersive Hofstadter minibands.
method: The study combines experimental measurements of Josephson current ($I_c$) and resistance ($R$) with detailed theoretical calculations based on the moiré Hamiltonian and band structure analysis.
model_or_system: The system is graphene/hBN moiré superlattices forming Josephson junctions. The physics is governed by the interplay between magnetic fields, the moiré potential, and superconducting proximity effects.
key_observables: Critical current ($I_c$), resistance ($R$), Fabry-Pérot oscillations, Fraunhofer interference patterns, and calculated average squared band velocity ($\langle v^2 angle$).
important_parameters: Magnetic field strength (up to 6 T), carrier density filling factor ($n/n_s$), superconducting gap ($\Delta$), and the magnetic flux quanta ($p/q$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes ballistic transport in the junctions, and theoretical calculations utilize approximations like block-diagonalization in valley space.
figures_summary: Figures show $R$ vs. density/field mapping out Landau fans evolving into Hofstadter butterfly spectra; $I_c$ measurements demonstrate high-field persistence; and supplementary figures detail band structures and calculated band velocities across various filling factors.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the experimental observation of high-field Josephson effects (Chunk 1) to analyzing the underlying physics in different regimes (semiclassical vs. moiré minibands, Chunk 2). It then delves into detailed theoretical calculations using the continuum model and magnetic translation symmetry to map band structure evolution (Chunks 3 & 4).
why_interesting: The mechanism relies on modifying electronic band structure via geometric potentials (moiré) to stabilize quantum coherence in extreme external fields, which is a rich topic connecting topology, superconductivity, and condensed matter theory.
